name: Chloe Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say is confidential and never traced back to you. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a litigator at Marlow Pierce, and most of my cases are defending insurance companies against injury claims: car crashes, falls in supermarkets, that kind of thing. My day is reading medical reports, preparing witness statements, and every week or two a short hearing in front of a judge. I use AI tools all day, for sorting thousands of documents, summarising medical records and drafting first versions of letters.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the hearings, honestly, standing up and making the argument. What wears me out is the volume: I carry about sixty files at once. The AI tools are the only reason I'm not working every weekend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be surprised, given what I use every day, but okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools were oversold but still worth having, and firms that use them well will win on price. At work I'd keep pushing the ones that work. Online I might write a short post on what actually saved time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd suit me. I'm already ahead on the tools, I get to keep doing hearings, and my job feels secure. The only real pressure is that insurers keep squeezing our fees, so the firm wants more files per lawyer every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going for senior associate and ask to take on more hearings and trials. I'd keep saving about 500 a month towards a house with Daniel. Maybe I'd start teaching the newer lawyers how to use the tools properly, which looks good at review time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit restless, maybe, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned insurers squeezing fees. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. Insurers pay us a fixed price per file now, so every hour the software saves goes to the client, not to my salary. But it's a business, and that's fair, so you find a way to be worth more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Daniel think about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel, my boyfriend, is an electrician and thinks my job is mostly reading, which isn't wrong. He jokes that I'll support him in a recession and he'll support me in a robot boom. We're very practical about money.

say: The tools were **oversold** but still worth having.
Firms that use them well will **win on price**, and I'd keep pushing those.
think: It'd suit me, since I'm **already ahead** on the tools and keep my hearings.
The real pressure is insurers **squeezing fees** and more files per lawyer.
do: Ask to take on **more hearings** and trials on the way to senior associate.
Save about **500 a month** towards a house with Daniel.
Teach newer lawyers to use the **tools properly**.
S0.quote: Insurers pay us a fixed price per file now, so every hour the software saves goes to the client, not to my salary.
fieldNote: Chloe treats the fee squeeze as **fair business**, fitting her free-market outlook.
She already carries **sixty files** and credits AI for her free weekends.
Her boyfriend's **hands-on trade** gives the household a different kind of risk.

steps.text: Ask for more hearings and trials this year
Save 500 a month towards a house with Daniel
Run AI tool training sessions for newer lawyers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next one. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one I can see already. Half of it is happening on my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for clients and good for lawyers who adapt. At work I'd volunteer to lead how we use AI on disclosure, the stage where both sides share their documents. Online I'd say the profession should stop moaning and get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the document side of my job, which is maybe half my week, goes to software fast. That means the firm needs fewer associates per partner, and I'm average, not a star. My hearings and my comfort with the tools are what keep me on the right side of the cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd make myself the person who runs disclosure with AI across the team, and I'd tell Graham, my supervising partner, that's what I want. I'd do an advocacy course so I can take bigger hearings. And I'd quietly start planning a small practice of my own for later, because AI makes running a two-person firm cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but energised. It's a race, and I like races.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're average. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, more than I'd say in the office. Being average was fine when the firm needed bodies, but now average lawyers are the ones the software replaces first. So I'd make sure I'm not average at the thing that matters next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go to a professional body or a group about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think lobbying fixes this. I'd rather the market sorts out who's useful, and I'd make sure I'm useful. That's how my parents raised me: work hard and don't wait for someone to save you.

say: This is **good for clients** and for lawyers who adapt.
I'd volunteer to lead AI use on **disclosure**, where both sides share documents.
think: The **document work**, about half my week, goes to software fast.

do: Lead the team's **AI disclosure** work and tell her supervising partner so.
Take an **advocacy course** to handle bigger hearings.
Start quietly planning a **small practice** of her own.
feel: **Uneasy but energised**, treating it like a race.

fieldNote: Chloe privately admits being **average** is her weak point, which she hides at work.
She rejects lobbying and trusts **the market** to reward useful people.
Her plan for a **two-person firm** shows a real appetite for risk.

steps.text: Lead AI-based disclosure across her litigation team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Right. Okay, give me a second.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say courts will still need humans for a good while, because judges and juries are people. I'd say the law moves slowly, and that's our protection. Online I'd keep quiet, because nobody wants a lawyer explaining why lawyers are fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the reading and writing part of my job is gone in two years, and that's most of it. Hearings might last a bit, but insurers would settle more claims by software and fewer would reach court. In 2028 I'd be a courtroom lawyer in a world that's suddenly stopped going to court.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. I'd leave the firm within the year and set up a tiny practice with AI doing the paperwork, taking small injury cases for people who can't afford a big firm. And I'd move in with Daniel now rather than in two years, to halve the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with my sleeves rolled up. I'd be scared on Sunday nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Daniel's work is hands-on. What does the three-year robot gap mean for your household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means Daniel's the safe one until about 2031, which is funny given he left school at sixteen. If my practice fails, his wage covers rent while I find the next thing. Then by 2031 the robots reach him too, and we'd both need a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Starting a firm with a few months of savings is a risk. Why not stay put?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because staying put means waiting for the letter. I'd rather spend my savings on something I own than on rent while I'm job hunting. My grandmother started a bakery with less.

say: Courts will need **humans** for a good while, because judges are people.
The law **moves slowly**, and that's our protection.
think: The **reading and writing** part of my job, most of it, goes in two years.
Insurers would **settle by software**, so fewer cases reach court.
do: Leave the firm within a year to set up a **tiny practice** run with AI.
Take **small injury cases** for people who can't afford big firms.
Move in with Daniel now to **halve the rent**.
S2.quote: In 2028 I'd be a courtroom lawyer in a world that's suddenly stopped going to court.
fieldNote: Chloe's answer to the fastest picture is to **start a business**, not to wait.
Daniel's trade makes him **the safe earner** until about 2031, which she finds funny.
She'd spend savings on **something she owns** rather than on job hunting.

steps.text: Leave Marlow Pierce within a year to open her own small practice
Run the new practice's paperwork with AI tools
Move in with Daniel now to halve the rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's a lot better for planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for a smart firm to rebuild itself, and that ours should start now. I'd offer to help design it. Publicly I'd say the profession will survive in a smaller form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me time to make senior associate, save more, and then jump with a name and some clients. It's still my whole desk job going in 2031. Five years is enough time to build a client list, and a client list is the one thing software can't copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Marlow Pierce for two or three years and take every hearing going. I'd save hard, 800 a month, and build relationships with the small claims firms that refer work. By 2029 I'd launch my own practice with one other lawyer, using AI for the paperwork from day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's a deadline, but a deadline I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change things with Daniel, like marriage or children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd marry next year, I think, because we're Catholic and we want a family. I'd want children before 2031, honestly, while I still have a steady wage and maternity pay. It's a strange reason to hurry, but it's a real one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you want as the other lawyer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone who's good in the courtroom and good with people, not a tech person, because I'm the tech person. Probably a woman I trained with who's now at a firm across town. We already joke about it.

say: A smart firm has **enough time** to rebuild, and ours should start now.
The profession will **survive** in a smaller form.
think: I'd make senior associate, then **jump with clients** and a name.
My **whole desk job** still goes in 2031.
do: Take **every hearing** going for two or three years.
Save **800 a month** and build ties with referral firms.
Launch **her own practice** with a courtroom partner by 2029.
feel: **Uneasy**, facing a deadline she feels she **can work with**.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time to build a client list, and a client list is the one thing software can't copy.
fieldNote: Chloe would bring **marriage and children** forward to fit before 2031.
She sees **client relationships** as the asset AI can't copy.
She'd partner with a courtroom lawyer and be **the tech person** herself.

steps.text: Save 800 a month while taking every hearing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's almost comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where the market works best, because there's time for people to retrain and businesses to adapt. I'd tell young lawyers to learn the tools and the courtroom both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I could build something real: a practice, a family, a house with Daniel. I'd be 37, with experience, which is a good age to run a firm. I'd still need to own something by 2036, not be someone's employee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the firm for four or five years, get to senior associate, and save. Then I'd open my own practice around 2031 and put real money into it. Daniel and I would buy a house in the next two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Excited, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots arrive around 2039. Does that change your long-term plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For Daniel it does. By 2039 his electrical work would be under pressure, so I'd want my practice to be the main earner by then. I want my own practice paying the bills before the robots reach my boyfriend's electrician van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything about this picture still unsettling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That everyone will be doing what I plan to do. If every average lawyer opens a small AI practice, prices crash. So I'd need to be known for something specific, probably injury cases for small businesses.

say: This is where the **market works best**, with time to retrain and adapt.
Young lawyers should learn the **tools** and the **courtroom** both.
think: Ten years lets me build a **practice, family and house**.
By 2036 I need to **own something**, not be someone's employee.
do: Stay at the firm **four or five years** and reach senior associate.
Buy **a house** with Daniel in the next two years.
S4.quote: I want my own practice paying the bills before the robots reach my boyfriend's electrician van.
fieldNote: Chloe sees the long timeline as **an opportunity**, fitting her free-market outlook.
She plans for her practice to **out-earn** Daniel's trade before robots reach it.
Her one worry is **everyone copying** her plan and crashing prices.

steps.text: Stay at Marlow Pierce and aim for senior associate
Buy a house with Daniel within two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to build a client list, and Daniel's wage would be the only thing between us and trouble. What would help is low barriers to starting a practice, like cheaper insurance and fewer fees, not handouts. Give me the freedom to compete and I'll find my own work, but don't make me pay a fortune just to open my own door.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people what they'd build, not just what they'd lose. Most conversations about this are about fear. Some of us are already planning.

headlineQuote: Give me the freedom to compete and I'll find my own work, but don't make me pay a fortune just to open my own door.
portrait: Chloe Torres is a 27-year-old **insurance-defence litigator** who uses AI every day and loves hearings.
She calls herself **average** in private and plans to stand out through courtroom and tool skills.
In faster pictures she'd **start her own practice** early, with AI running its paperwork.
Her boyfriend Daniel's **electrician work** gives the household time, since robots arrive later.
She trusts **the market** over lobbying and wants freedom to compete, not handouts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no time to build a client list and Daniel's wage the only buffer.
whatWouldHelp: **Lower barriers** to starting a practice, such as cheaper insurance and fewer fees.
